summary: Specifies what a host's Internet Protocol implementation must do to support multicasting, sending one datagram to a group of machines. It supersedes RFC 966, which explains the motivation, and was a proposed standard. It was in turn replaced by RFC 1054 and RFC 1112.

eli5.summary: Instead of calling each friend one by one, you shout once and everyone who joined the group hears you. This memo says what a computer must do to join such groups.

questions: what are host extensions for ip multicasting
how does ip multicast work for hosts
how do hosts join a multicast group
how is multicast different from broadcast
subtitle: How IP hosts join and send to groups using the same message.

tldr.problem: IP in the early 1980s could only send messages one-to-one (unicast). Some applications needed to send a single message to a group of receivers at once, avoiding the overhead of sending copies to each one individually.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 988 specifies how a host IP implementation must support multicast by recognizing Class D IP addresses as group addresses, allowing hosts to join groups and receive datagrams sent to those groups. It defines three conformance levels: Level 0 (no multicast), Level 1 (send only), and Level 2 (send and receive).
tldr.outcome: Multicast became fundamental to Internet protocols like resource discovery and live video streaming. This specification was refined and replaced by RFC 1054 and RFC 1112 with improvements.

today: RFC 988 is now superseded by RFC 1054 and RFC 1112, which refined the multicast specification. IP multicast remains in use today for applications like Internet Protocol Television (IPTV), video conferencing, and discovery protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IP multicasting is the transmission of an IP datagram to a host group—a set of zero or more hosts identified by a single IP destination address. A multicast datagram is delivered to all members of the destination host group with the same best-efforts reliability as regular IP datagrams: it is not guaranteed to arrive, and datagrams may arrive out of order.

Host group membership is dynamic: hosts join and leave groups at any time, with no restriction on the location or number of members. A host may belong to multiple groups simultaneously. Importantly, a host need not be a member of a group to send datagrams to it. Groups can be permanent (administratively assigned addresses) or transient (dynamically created and destroyed).
sections.eli5: A multicast group is like a chatroom that computers can join. When someone sends a message to the group, everyone in it receives it, but nobody has to be in the group to send to it.

sections.title: Conformance Levels
sections.content:
RFC 988 defines three levels of support for IP multicasting, allowing implementations to add multicast support incrementally.

Level 0 means no multicast support. Level 0 hosts are generally unaffected by multicast activity, except that they must learn to discard datagrams destined to Class D addresses. Level 1 hosts can send multicast datagrams but cannot receive them or join groups, allowing them to participate in multicast-based services like resource location. Level 2 hosts have full support: they can create, join and leave host groups, send and receive multicast datagrams, and must implement the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP).
sections.eli5: There are three levels of skill: beginners who ignore groups, people who can shout to a group, and experts who can shout and also join groups to listen.

sections.title: Host Architecture and Multicast Agents
sections.content:
The RFC specifies multicast extensions in terms of a layered model. At Level 2, a host IP implementation must provide three new services: sending multicast datagrams, receiving multicast datagrams, and managing group membership. These services extend the IP service interface, the IP module itself, and the local network service interface (e.g., Ethernet).

Multicast agents are special entities in internet gateways that manage the creation of transient groups and group membership information. There is at least one multicast agent directly attached to every IP network or subnetwork that supports multicasting. When a host sends a multicast datagram, it transmits it to a local network multicast address. If the group has members on other networks, multicast agents relay the datagram to other agents and networks, ensuring that all members receive it.
sections.eli5: Each network has a special computer (an agent) that helps manage the groups and makes sure messages reach members on other networks. Regular computers don't do this job—the agents handle it.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Multicast Datagrams
sections.content:
To send multicast datagrams, the IP module must recognize Class D addresses and send them to the local network instead of through a gateway. If the sending host is itself a member of the destination group, a copy must be looped back locally (if loopback was requested when joining the group). Hosts with multiple network interfaces must transmit multicast datagrams on exactly one interface, leaving delivery to other networks to multicast agents.

To receive multicast datagrams, the IP module must recognize the addresses of groups to which the host belongs and deliver incoming datagrams destined to those group addresses. Datagrams destined to groups the host does not belong to are silently discarded. ICMP error messages are never generated in response to multicast datagrams.
sections.eli5: To send, a computer just puts the group address on the message. To receive, a computer keeps track of which groups it joined and accepts messages only for those groups.

sections.title: Group Membership Management
sections.content:
The RFC defines three operations for managing group membership: CreateGroup requests creation of a new transient host group (specifying whether it is private or public, and whether loopback is enabled), JoinGroup requests membership in an existing group, and LeaveGroup requests departure from a group. These operations are supported by the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP), which is specified in an appendix.

Group membership is per-host, not per-process. The IP module maintains a data structure listing all host groups to which the host currently belongs, along with each group's loopback policy and access key. Multicast agents confirm host membership periodically using a "deadman timer" procedure.
sections.eli5: Computers use special messages to ask to join, create, or leave groups. A special protocol called IGMP handles these requests and makes sure the agents know who is in each group.

sections.title: Host Group Addresses and Local Network Mapping
sections.content:
Host groups are identified by Class D IP addresses (those with the high-order four bits "1110"). For Ethernet networks, RFC 988 specifies that an IP host group address is mapped to an Ethernet multicast address by placing the low-order 28 bits of the IP address into the low-order 28 bits of an Ethernet address. The high-order 20 bits of the Ethernet address are set to a well-known value.

The RFC notes that other network types can use similar mappings. For networks that do not natively support multicast (like the ARPANET), all IP host group addresses can be mapped to a single local broadcast or to a multicast agent's address.
sections.eli5: Class D addresses (starting with 1110 in binary) are reserved for groups. On Ethernet, these IP group addresses get translated to special Ethernet addresses that the hardware understands.
